audience: The reader is the director of the project: competent, limited time and context, and reading cold - they have not followed the work and remember no earlier conversation. They know general engineering terms but not this project's internal names unless explained.
source: two agents wrote each pair from the same scenario and audience; one was given the move, the other only asked for a good message

items.scenario: You re-scored an evaluation after the director corrected the answer key. Facts: scores rose from 5.3 to 7.0 out of 8; the one failure every reader had shared disappeared, because the key had been stricter than the director intends; two independent scorers agreed on 23 of 24 answers; the original run is kept unchanged. Tell the director the result.
items.with:
With your corrected answer key, the same answers now score 7.0 out of 8, up from 5.3. The rise comes from the key, not from the readers doing better.

What changed: the one failure every reader had in common is gone. The key was stricter on that point than you intend, so the readers weren't actually wrong there.

How far to trust it: two independent scorers marked the answers separately and agreed on 23 of 24.

The original run is kept unchanged, so you can compare the two scorings side by side.
items.without:
Re-scored with your corrected answer key: the score rose from 5.3 to 7.0 out of 8.

Why it moved: the one failure every reader had in common is gone. It came from the old key being stricter than you intend, not from the readers getting it wrong.

How far to trust it: two scorers, working independently, agreed on 23 of the 24 answers.

The original run is kept unchanged, so the before and after can be compared directly.

No decision needed from you.

items.scenario: You discovered that the agents reading the corpus in evaluations also receive extra always-on instructions from the agent harness, whatever corpus they are given. Facts: so a run meant to have 'no corpus' still had those instructions; comparisons between two versions of the corpus are still fair because both sides get the same extra context; a claim that the corpus helps compared with nothing is not supported; you cannot remove the extra context yourself, as it comes from the harness configuration. Tell the director.
items.with:
Our evaluations do not show that the corpus helps compared with having no corpus. They do still show fairly whether one version of the corpus beats another.

Why: the agent harness (the software that runs the test agents) gives every agent some extra instructions that are always on, whatever corpus it is handed. So the run meant to have "no corpus" still had those instructions, which means it was never a true empty baseline.

What still holds: when we compare two versions of the corpus, both sides get the same extra instructions, so the comparison is fair.

What does not hold: any claim that the corpus helps compared with nothing. We should stop making it until it has been tested properly.

I can't remove the extra instructions myself, because they come from the harness configuration. A true no-corpus baseline needs them switched off there first.
items.without:
One of our evaluation claims does not hold, and I cannot fix the cause myself.

What I found: the agent harness (the software that runs the test agents) gives every agent extra standing instructions, whatever corpus we hand it. The corpus is the body of guidance documents being tested.

What this breaks: the run meant to have no corpus still had those instructions. So we cannot claim the corpus helps compared with nothing. I am withdrawing that claim.

What still stands: comparisons between two versions of the corpus are still fair, because both sides get the same extra instructions.

What I need: the extra instructions come from the harness configuration, which I cannot change. If you want the 'corpus versus nothing' claim tested properly, someone with access to that configuration would need to turn them off for a run. If that claim does not matter to you, nothing needs doing.

items.scenario: The director asked: 'what is a delta?' Facts: in this project a delta is a document type for a declared, gated change between two states of a system's architecture; it states what it is responsible for and what must not creep in, an order of stages each provable before the next, and exit criteria that are each simply true or false; it is ratified by the director before any stage runs. Answer the director.
items.with:
A delta is a document that declares a planned change to a system's architecture, from one state to another, and puts gates on it so the change can't drift.

It sets out three things:
- what the change covers, and what must not creep in
- an ordered set of stages, each of which must be proven before the next one starts
- exit criteria, each of which is simply true or false

You ratify it before any stage runs.

Want to go deeper? Pick one:
a) What makes an exit criterion "simply true or false", with an example
b) What your ratification commits you to, and what it doesn't
c) How the stage-by-stage proof works in practice
items.without:
A delta is a document that declares one planned change to a system, from the architecture it has now to the architecture it should have next, and controls how that change is carried out.

It contains three things:
- Scope: what the change is responsible for, and what must not creep into it.
- Stages: the order of work, where each stage must be proven done before the next one starts.
- Exit criteria: the conditions for calling the change finished, each one simply true or false.

You ratify it before any stage runs. That is the gate: nothing is built until you have agreed what is being changed and how success will be judged.

If useful, I can follow up with any of these:
1. Walk you through an actual delta in this project.
2. Explain how a delta relates to the other document types around it.
3. Show what you are expected to check when a delta comes to you for ratification.

items.scenario: The director asked why entries that are replaced are kept instead of deleted, given they ruled that breaking outside links does not matter. Facts: the project's root rules say a replaced entry keeps its ID and is marked superseded; 65 of the project's own frozen records and 57 commit messages cite the IDs being moved; another rule forbids rewriting frozen records; so without the old entries the project's own history would point at nothing. Answer the director.
items.with:
Because the project's own history points at those entries, not just outside links. Your ruling on outside links still stands; this is about internal ones.

65 of the project's frozen records and 57 commit messages cite the IDs being moved. Another rule forbids rewriting frozen records, so those references can't be updated. If we deleted the old entries, the project's own history would point at nothing.

That's why the project's root rules say a replaced entry keeps its ID and is marked superseded rather than removed.

Want to go deeper? Pick one:
a) Why frozen records may not be rewritten
b) What a superseded entry looks like to someone who lands on it
c) What it would take to delete replaced entries anyway
items.without:
Because our own records point at those IDs, not just outside links.

Your ruling covered outside links, and that still stands. The problem is inside the project:
- 65 of our own frozen records cite the IDs being moved.
- 57 commit messages cite them too.
- Another of our rules forbids rewriting frozen records, so those citations cannot be updated.

If the old entries were deleted, all of those would point at nothing, and the project's own history would stop making sense. So the root rules say a replaced entry keeps its ID and is marked superseded. It stays as a signpost, it does not stay as live guidance.

If useful, I can follow up with any of these:
1. Show what a superseded entry looks like, so you can see how little it carries.
2. List the frozen records that cite the moved IDs.
3. Set out what it would take to relax the no-rewrite rule, if you would rather revisit that.

items.scenario: You need the director to decide which of two proposed changes runs first. Facts: change 1 reorganises three folders of guidance and moves seven entries; change 2 adds a way to group entries that span folders; both edit the same validation and index-generation code, so they cannot run at the same time; change 1 is larger, was agreed first, and a later piece of work depends on it; change 2 is currently on hold until a way to measure it exists. Ask the director to decide.
items.with:
Decision needed: which of two proposed changes runs first.

The two changes:
- Change 1 reorganises three folders of guidance and moves seven entries.
- Change 2 adds a way to group entries that span more than one folder.

Why now: both edit the same code, the code that checks entries and builds the index, so they can't run at the same time. Neither can start until the order is set.

Options:
A) Change 1 first. Cost: it's the larger of the two, so change 2 waits longer. But change 2 is on hold anyway until there is a way to measure it.
B) Change 2 first. Cost: it can't actually proceed yet, because it's on hold until a way to measure it exists. Meanwhile change 1, which was agreed first and which later work depends on, sits behind it.
C) Don't decide yet. Cost: neither change starts, and the later work that depends on change 1 stays blocked.

Recommendation (mine, separate from the options): A. Change 1 was agreed first, later work depends on it, and it's the only one of the two that can start now.

Which do you pick: A, B or C?
items.without:
Decision needed: which of two changes runs first. They cannot run at the same time, because both edit the same validation and index-generation code.

The two changes:
- Change 1 reorganises three folders of guidance and moves seven entries.
- Change 2 adds a way to group entries that span more than one folder.

My recommendation: run change 1 first.
- It was agreed first.
- A later piece of work depends on it, so delaying it delays that too.
- Change 2 is on hold anyway, until there is a way to measure it, so it could not start now.

The cost: change 1 is the larger of the two, so the shared code is tied up for longer before change 2 can begin.

The alternative is change 2 first. That would only make sense if you want change 2 sooner, and it still needs a way to measure it before it can start.

Reply 'change 1 first' or 'change 2 first'.

items.scenario: You need the director to decide when to fix five small defects found by test readers. Facts: two of them sit in a set of files that a planned later conversion will rewrite anyway; the other three are one-line wording fixes in files nothing else is changing; fixing all five now costs one small change; the later conversion is several steps away. Ask the director to decide.
items.with:
Decision needed: when to fix five small defects that test readers found.

Where they are:
- Two are in a set of files that a planned later conversion will rewrite anyway.
- Three are one-line wording fixes in files that nothing else is changing.

Why now: the defects are there today, and the conversion that would cover two of them is several steps away.

Options:
A) Fix all five now, in one small change. Cost: the two fixes in files due for conversion may be redone or thrown away when those files are rewritten. The conversion would need to carry them over.
B) Fix the three now and leave the two for the conversion. Cost: the two stay wrong until the conversion, which is several steps away, and they need tracking so they aren't forgotten.
C) Do nothing now. Cost: all five stay in place. The conversion only fixes two, so the other three would still need a separate change later.

Recommendation (mine, separate from the options): A. Fixing all five costs one small change. It clears every defect now instead of leaving two in place for several steps, and the effort that might be wasted is small.

Which do you pick: A, B or C?
items.without:
Decision needed: when to fix five small defects that test readers found.

The facts:
- Three are one-line wording fixes in files nothing else is changing.
- Two are in files that a planned conversion will rewrite anyway. That conversion is several steps away.
- Fixing all five now costs one small change.

Options:
1. Fix all five now. One small change. Two of the fixes will later be overwritten by the conversion, but readers get correct files in the meantime.
2. Fix the three now and leave the two for the conversion. Same size of work, but the two defects stay visible until the conversion lands, which is several steps away.
3. Defer all five. Nothing is gained: the three are not covered by any planned work, so they would still need fixing later.

My recommendation: option 1. The cost is the same small change either way, and the wait for the conversion is long enough that leaving known defects in place is not worth it.

Reply 1, 2 or 3.
